# Draft:Monument of the Battle of Musa Dagh (Musaler)

The Monument of the Battle of Musa Dagh (Armenian: Մուսա լեռան հերոսամարտի հուշահամալիր, Musa Leran Hushahamalir) is a memorial in Musaler, Armavir Province, Armenia, dedicated to the Armenian resistance during the Battle of Musa Dagh in 1915, a significant event of the Armenian Genocide. Erected in 1976, the monument commemorates the 53-day defense by approximately 5,000–6,000 Armenians from six villages against Ottoman forces, which inspired Franz Werfel’s novel The Forty Days of Musa Dagh.
History
The Battle of Musa Dagh occurred from July to September 1915, when Armenians from six villages—Kabusia, Yoghunoluk, Bitias, Vakef, Kheter Bey, and Haji Habibli—in the Hatay Province of modern-day Turkey resisted Ottoman deportation orders during the Armenian Genocide. Led by figures like Movses Der Kalousdian, the defenders held Musa Dagh (Mount Moses) for 53 days until their rescue by French warships on 12 September 1915. The monument was constructed to honor this act of defiance and survival, reflecting the Armenian diaspora’s resilience.
Construction began in 1976, with the monument’s opening on 16 September of that year. Designed by architect Rafael Israelyan and sculptor Ara Harutyunyan, it is built from red tufa stone, symbolizing strength and endurance. Located on a hill in Musaler, near Yerevan’s Zvartnots airport, the monument includes a museum detailing the battle and an ethnographic museum in the village depicting life in Musa Dagh’s villages.
Design and Symbolism
The monument’s fortress-like structure, crafted from red tufa, evokes the defensive spirit of the Musa Dagh resistance. Its inscription, “To the heroic self-defense battle of Musa Ler,” underscores the Armenians’ 53-day stand. The design integrates elements of Armenian sacred architecture, with its stark, imposing form symbolizing courage and survival. A statue of Franz Werfel, author of The Forty Days of Musa Dagh, stands nearby, acknowledging the novel’s role in globalizing the event’s significance.
Cultural Significance
The monument is a pilgrimage site, particularly during annual commemorations in September, which include cooking harisa, a traditional dish of wheat and meat that sustained the 1915 defenders. Only 14 Musaler families, with the privilege passed patrilineally, prepare harisa for the event, symbolizing continuity. The celebrations feature music, dance, and speeches, often attended by dignitaries like the mayor of Anjar, Lebanon, where many Musa Dagh survivors resettled. The French flag flies alongside Armenia’s, honoring the 1915 rescue by French warships.
The monument is one of four memorials to the Musa Dagh resistance, alongside those in Damlajik, Turkey (1932, now in ruins), Canada (1989), and a planned site in Syria. Its cultural impact extends beyond Armenia, inspiring resistance movements, notably in Jewish ghettos during the Holocaust, where Werfel’s novel was circulated.
